lead: An operating system relies on hardware interrupts to respond immediately to external physical events without wasting central processing unit (CPU) time. An interrupt is an electrical signal sent by hardware to alter the instruction execution sequence of the processor. Computer-system architectures range from single-processor systems to symmetric multiprocessors and multi-node clusters. Interrupt-driven handling and Direct Memory Access (DMA) allow input/output (I/O) device controllers to transfer data directly to main memory, preventing the CPU from freezing in busy-waiting polling loops.
prereq: You need: basic understanding of hardware components from 1.1 Role of an OS and computer-system organization.

blocks.text: Computer systems are categorized by the number of general-purpose processing units built into the system hardware.

items: Single-processor systems: The system has one main CPU capable of executing a general-purpose instruction set. Devices like disk controllers or graphics adapters may contain microprocessors, but they do not run general-purpose system processes.

Multiprocessor systems: Also called parallel systems or multicore systems, these contain two or more CPUs sharing the system bus, clock, memory, and peripheral hardware. Multiprocessing increases system throughput, improves reliability through fault tolerance, and achieves economies of scale.

Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP): The dominant multiprocessor architecture. Each processor runs an identical copy of the operating system. Processors communicate across the shared system bus, and any processor can execute user or kernel tasks.

Clustered systems: Two or more individual computer systems (nodes) are linked together over a high-speed local area network (LAN) or storage area network (SAN). Clusters share storage arrays to provide high-availability processing and high-performance computing.

sections.h3: Hardware interrupts, software traps, and vectors

blocks.text: An interrupt alerts the CPU to a hardware or software condition requiring attention.

items: An external hardware device (like a keyboard, network card, or timer) asserts an Interrupt Request (IRQ) physical line connected to the CPU or interrupt controller.
The CPU finishes executing its current instruction, pushes the current Program Counter (PC) and processor status register onto the system stack, and disables lower-priority interrupts.
The CPU fetches an integer vector number provided by the interrupt controller.

The CPU uses the vector number to index into an array of function pointers stored in low memory. In 16-bit real mode, this array is the Interrupt Vector Table (IVT). In 32-bit/64-bit protected mode, it is the Interrupt Descriptor Table (IDT).
The CPU loads the program counter with the address of the corresponding Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) retrieved from the IVT/IDT and begins executing the ISR handler code.

The ISR processes the device event, clears the interrupt condition register on the device, and executes an Interrupt Return instruction (such as IRET in x86). The CPU restores saved registers and resumes the interrupted instruction stream.

blocks.text: Interrupts fall into two primary mechanical categories: hardware interrupts and software traps.

head: Property
Hardware Interrupt
Software Trap / Exception
rows: Internal CPU execution (div-by-zero, page fault, system call instruction)
Asynchronous (can happen at any clock tick)
Synchronous (occurs at the exact execution of the faulting instruction)
Can be masked via interrupt flags (except NMI)
Cannot be masked; must be handled or process terminates

blocks.text: The CPU uses an interrupt priority system and a mask register to control handling order. Non-Maskable Interrupts (NMI) bypass masking and are reserved for unrecoverable hardware errors like memory parity failures or power brownouts.

sections.h3: I/O techniques: polling, interrupt-driven I/O, and Direct Memory Access (DMA)

blocks.text: Input and output operations require transferring data between main RAM memory and peripheral device controllers. Systems use three main control mechanisms.

items: Programmed I/O (Polling): The CPU continuously reads an I/O controller status register in a tight loop until a busy bit clears. This busy-waiting burns CPU cycles that could execute other active programs.

Interrupt-Driven I/O: The CPU issues an I/O command to the device controller and immediately switches to executing another process. When the device controller completes the read or write, it signals a hardware interrupt. The CPU handles the transfer inside an ISR and returns to execution.
Direct Memory Access (DMA): Interrupt-driven I/O produces high CPU overhead for bulk block transfers because an interrupt fires for every byte or word transferred. DMA solves this bottleneck.
The device driver program writes the memory buffer start address, transfer byte count, and control flags into the DMA controller registers.
The CPU resumes running other user processes.
The DMA controller manages the system bus directly, copying data blocks between the hardware device buffer and RAM without sending bytes through CPU registers.
When the entire memory block transfer finishes, the DMA controller issues a single hardware interrupt to notify the CPU that the transfer is complete.

figure.caption: Hardware interrupt handling sequence: the device controller signals the CPU, which saves context, fetches the handler vector address, executes the ISR, clears the device status, and restores processor state.

examples.question: A hard disk controller transfers a 4 KB block to RAM. The physical read operation takes 5 ms (5000 µs) to complete. In a polling system, the CPU continuously checks the status register every 0.2 µs, wasting CPU time for the entire duration. In an interrupt-driven system, the CPU issues the read command, switches to another process, and receives a hardware interrupt when the read completes. The ISR execution and context switch overhead total 4 µs. Calculate: (a) CPU time wasted in pure polling, (b) CPU time spent handling the interrupt in the interrupt-driven approach, and (c) net CPU time saved by using interrupts instead of polling.
steps: Step 1: Total time required for disk physical read operation T_disk = 5 ms = 5000 µs.
Step 2: Calculate CPU time wasted during polling. The CPU busy-waits continuously for the entire duration of the disk read: T_polling = 5000 µs.
Step 3: Calculate CPU time spent handling the interrupt-driven approach. The CPU spent time is limited to context switching and running the ISR: T_interrupt = 4 µs.
Step 4: Calculate net CPU time saved. T_saved = T_polling - T_interrupt = 5000 µs - 4 µs = 4996 µs (or 4.996 ms).
examples.answer: The CPU time wasted in pure polling is 5000.0 µs, the interrupt overhead is 4.0 µs, and the net saved CPU time is 4996.0 µs.
examples.check:
polling_time_us = 5000.0
interrupt_overhead_us = 4.0
saved_time_us = polling_time_us - interrupt_overhead_us
print(f"{polling_time_us:.1f}")
print(f"{interrupt_overhead_us:.1f}")
print(f"{saved_time_us:.1f}")

traps: Treating software traps and hardware interrupts as identical: hardware interrupts are asynchronous signals triggered by external physical components, whereas traps/exceptions are synchronous events caused directly by executing an instruction (such as divide by zero).

Assuming Direct Memory Access (DMA) completely eliminates interrupts: DMA eliminates per-byte interrupts during high-speed transfers, but it still triggers one final completion interrupt per block transfer.

Believing the Interrupt Vector Table (IVT) contains actual handler code: the IVT/IDT holds memory addresses (pointers or descriptors) pointing to where ISR code begins, not the machine instructions of the ISR itself.

Thinking maskable interrupts block Non-Maskable Interrupts (NMI): clearing the interrupt flag bit in the status register blocks standard maskable hardware lines (IRQ), but does not block critical NMI pins.

quiz.q: What table holds memory addresses of Interrupt Service Routines in x86 protected mode?
Explain why programmed I/O (polling) causes high overhead in single-core general-purpose computing.
quiz.a: Polling forces the CPU into a tight busy-waiting loop, continuously checking an I/O controller status register. This prevents the CPU from executing useful instructions for other active processes during slow hardware operations.

quiz.q: Why does Direct Memory Access (DMA) increase system efficiency during bulk block data transfers compared to interrupt-driven I/O?
quiz.a: Standard interrupt-driven I/O generates one CPU interrupt per transferred byte or word, creating massive context-switch overhead. DMA transfers an entire memory block directly into RAM without CPU register intervention and issues only a single interrupt upon block completion.

quiz.q: A system receives a hardware interrupt while processing a critical kernel routine with interrupts disabled (masked). Describe what happens to the incoming hardware interrupt signal.
quiz.a: The hardware interrupt request (IRQ) line remains latched at the interrupt controller level. The CPU ignores the signal until the kernel re-enables interrupts by clearing the mask flag bit, at which point the CPU acknowledges and processes the pending interrupt.

quiz.q: Compare programmed I/O, interrupt-driven I/O, and DMA for a network card receiving a 1 MB file. State the total number of CPU interrupts generated under interrupt-driven I/O (1 byte per interrupt) versus DMA (1 block per transfer).
quiz.a: In programmed I/O, 0 interrupts occur, but CPU busy-waits for 100% of the transfer time. In interrupt-driven I/O (1 byte per interrupt), 1 MB = 1,048,576 interrupts fire, creating severe context-switching overhead. In DMA, only 1 hardware interrupt fires when the entire 1 MB block transfer completes.

beyond: Not for the exam. High-speed network interfaces (100 Gbps Ethernet) can trigger millions of interrupts per second, causing an overload known as an interrupt storm. Operating systems use hybrid techniques like Linux NAPI (New API) or DPDK (Data Plane Development Kit), which dynamically disable hardware interrupts during high packet arrival rates and temporarily switch to adaptive polling. Modern PCI Express buses also replace physical IRQ wires with Message Signaled Interrupts (MSI and MSI-X) sent directly as memory write packets across the bus. Search for 'Linux NAPI adaptive polling', 'PCIe MSI-X', and 'DPDK zero-copy kernel bypass' to learn more.
